commit.message:
fix(worker): preserve reconciled files during fast-forward (#137942)

At turn start a cloud worker fast-forwards its checkout to the session branch. When an incoming commit changed a path's shape (file to directory or the reverse) and the worker had a local file or directory at that path, the fast-forward moved HEAD and the index but could not materialize the incoming files, leaving the checkout half-advanced.

The GitHub checkout binder now checks the components of each incoming added path before the reset and skips the whole fast-forward with a warning when a local file or directory obstructs one, preserving the local branch, index, and working-tree bytes even for clean tracked blockers. Native path lookup also catches case and Unicode aliases on filesystems that fold them.

Related: #137011

Co-authored-by: zhang-guiping <zhang.guiping@xydigit.com>

commit.message:
fix: handle uppercase finish reasons from compatible Gemini endpoints (#188269)

fix(ai): map uppercase STOP and MAX_TOKENS finish reasons on OpenAI-compatible endpoints

Some OpenAI-compatible endpoints (for example Gemini-backed ones) return uppercase `finish_reason` values in Chat Completions JSON and SSE. The stop-reason mapper didn't know `STOP` or `MAX_TOKENS`. As a result, `STOP` turned a normal reply into an error. The completions transport also stored the raw value, so a reply cut off at `MAX_TOKENS` was not treated as a length stop and its unfinished text was kept. The mapper now maps `STOP` to stop and `MAX_TOKENS` to length, and the transport uses the mapped value. `SAFETY` stays a raw error.

Evidence: built Gateway turns through the normal ModelRegistry `createLlmRuntime` producer against Chat Completions JSON and SSE fixtures, twice per case. With `MAX_TOKENS`, main kept the unfinished text and failed; with this change the text was withheld, the existing context recovery ran, and only the complete reply was returned. Uppercase `STOP` failed on main and succeeded with this change. Lowercase `stop` worked and `SAFETY` stayed a raw error on both refs. Details: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/188269#issuecomment-6522158245.

Thanks @ooiuuii.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

commit.message:
fix(anthropic): stop reporting success after OpenClaw MCP startup fails (#176154)

fix(anthropic): fail the Claude CLI turn when the openclaw MCP server fails to start

Fixes #176138.

When the Gateway was slow to answer and Claude Code's own 5-second MCP connect timeout expired, Claude reported the openclaw MCP server as `failed` in its `system/init` message. OpenClaw ignored that, so the turn ran without any OpenClaw tools and still reported success. OpenClaw now checks the init message, ends the session through the existing closeSession path and reports a startup failure with retry guidance.

Evidence: real Claude Code 2.1.309 routed through a trusted-CA HTTPS CONNECT fixture (no login, no paid key) with built Gateways. A delayed Gateway MCP dispatch produced `system/init.mcp_servers: [{name:"openclaw",status:"failed"}]`. Main reported success with 0 tool calls (twice); with this change the turn exited with the startup failure and retry guidance (twice). With a normal connect, both refs ran ToolSearch and a Gateway-backed Read with the file contents. Details: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/176154#issuecomment-6522021568.

Thanks @xyi74976-del.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

commit.message:
fix(channels): preserve IRC timing and Teams uploads across clock changes (#188293)

fix(irc,msteams): measure in-process durations with a monotonic clock

IRC and Microsoft Teams measured some in-process durations with wall-clock time, so a system clock jump changed them:
- the IRC probe latency could be wrong;
- IRC reconnect backoff reset too early or not at all;
- a fresh Teams file-consent upload could expire too early.

These durations now use `performance.now()`. Persisted dates and public `createdAt` timestamps are unchanged, and so are the budgets.

Evidence: built Gateway, main twice and candidate twice, with `Date.now` stepped inside the process only. Main reproduced the wrong probe latency, the wrong reconnect resets and the early expiry of a fresh Teams upload; the candidate corrected all three. The Teams path ran authenticated consent invokes, exact-byte uploads and the original card update. Controls passed: normal timing and expiry, invalid JWT, conversation mismatch and decline. Details: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/188293#issuecomment-6521663467.

Includes the fixes from #188237, #188238 and #188239, with their commits kept.

Co-authored-by: Claude Code <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix(exec): require approval for legacy arithmetic arguments (#187653)

* fix(exec): gate legacy $[...] arithmetic arguments in allowlist mode

Bash re-evaluates the text of a `$[...]` arithmetic expansion, so an array
subscript rebuilt from ANSI-C numeric escapes can run command substitution
even though no literal `$(` appears in the source. The shell authorization
plan already blocked `$((...))` dynamic arguments but its expansion pattern
missed the legacy `$[` form, so quoted `"$[...]"` operands on safe builtins
such as `:` and `cd` were auto-allowed and executed unchanged.

Treat `$[` like the other runtime shell expansions so these commands fall
back to approval.

* test(exec): verify arithmetic arguments stop before process launch

commit.message:
fix(exec): require approval for recursive shell assignments (#187499)

* fix(exec): require approval for recursively evaluated shell assignments

Standalone assignments added no step or risk to the shell planner, but bash evaluates arithmetic, braced parameter expansion, and subscripted names recursively, so an allowlisted trailing step could hide arbitrary execution. Flag those assignments as unanalyzable, and treat NAME+=value cmd as an environment prelude like NAME=value cmd.

Shell word text decoding and exec authorization risk classification move to sibling modules so the touched files stay within the line-cap ratchet.

* test(exec): prove recursive assignments stop before spawn

* fix(exec): block keyed compound assignments

* fix(exec): cover keyed array append entries

* fix(exec): remove stale lint suppressions

* chore(exec): prune stale line baselines

commit.message:
fix(telegram): bot-to-bot replies are not bounded by bot-loop protection (#151924)

fix(telegram): feed peer-bot facts into the shared bot-loop guard

When two bots in a Telegram group answered each other through Bot API bot-to-bot messaging, the shared bot-loop guard never received the peer-bot facts that Telegram supplies, so it could not count or stop the loop. Telegram turns now pass those facts to the existing guard. With the existing budget, the guard suppresses further peer input, logs a diagnostic and restores the reaction acknowledgment. Human messages are unaffected. There is no new config, SDK surface or counter.

Note: the default budget (20 per 60s) still allows the slow historical loop that was reported; a configured or faster loop is stopped.

Evidence: Telegram Test Server with two Convex-leased bots in one group, running built OpenClaw. With a configured budget, main went past it twice and the guard saw no peer-bot facts. With this change the third peer input was suppressed (twice), with the diagnostic logged and the acknowledgment restored, which Telegram accepted. A human message got exactly one reply on both refs. Details: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/151924#issuecomment-6520370049.

Thanks @amittell.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

commit.message:
test(plugins): guard the manifest half of live listing and new thinking hooks (#188227)

## What Problem This Solves

Two provider rules were written down but not checked, and Particle (#187135) hit the first one: its plugin could list the account's models, but without manifest `modelCatalog.discovery` the Gateway never refreshed it, so only catalog rows appeared.

## What Changed

- `provider-live-listing.contract.test.ts`: a hosted OpenAI-compatible provider that lists models live must also declare `modelCatalog.discovery.<provider>` as `refreshable` or `runtime`. The failure names the fix.
- `catalog-thinking-profiles.contract.test.ts`: the 24 plugins that still resolve thinking in code are listed. The test inspects real hooks (the provider contract registry, plus a `resolveThinkingProfile` export from the plugin's `provider-policy-api.ts`, which the resolver loads), not source text. A new plugin that adds a hook fails and is pointed at `compat.defaultThinkingLevel` / `compat.thinkingLevels`. Removing a hook requires removing its entry, so the list only shrinks.

## User Impact

None. Tests only.

## Proof

- Both tests pass on main.
- Removing Particle's `modelCatalog.discovery` fails the live-listing test with "particle: set modelCatalog.discovery.particle to \"refreshable\"".
- Adding a `resolveThinkingProfile` export to a Particle `provider-policy-api.ts` fails the hook test with the extra `particle` entry; a comment mentioning the name does not.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

commit.message:
feat(model-catalog): rows can state their offered thinking levels; xAI rows own their profiles (#188158)

## What Problem This Solves

A catalog row could only describe its thinking ladder indirectly (map plus efforts). When a provider's wire map aliases a level the picker should hide, or a row has no default, the profile still needed a provider hook.

## What Changed

- New compat field `compat.thinkingLevels`: the offered ladder, in order. A row that sets it (or `compat.defaultThinkingLevel`) owns its thinking profile; core runs it through the same normalizer as hook profiles, and provider hooks do not run. Compat-only, so released readers drop it.
- `ownsThinkingProfile` is the one ownership check, used by the resolver, the hosted-catalog planner and configured-map merging.
- xAI: the six bundled Grok rows state their ladder and default; they resolve exactly as the hook did. The hook stays for Grok releases not yet in the catalog and for subscription-listed rows.
- Provider rules and the provider PR checklist each gain one line on the field.

## User Impact

None. Offered levels and defaults are unchanged.

## Proof

- `pnpm catalog:compare-released` (2026.10.9, 2026.9.36, 2026.10.10-beta.5): no behavior change.
- `catalog-thinking-profiles.contract.test.ts`: the six Grok rows resolve to the hook's profiles with a deliberately wrong hook registered.
- `thinking.test.ts`: a stated ladder owns the profile without a default, and the hook does not run.
- Upgrade from 2026.10.9 on isolated state (sandboxed HOME/OPENCLAW_HOME/OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR, keys from env refs): released Gateway stores a `kimi/k3 --thinking low` session; after `doctor --fix`, this head's Gateway validates the config, resumes the session at `low`, and runs `moonshot/kimi-k3` at `max`. The new field is compat-only and optional, so stored config and sessions need no migration.

- Review follow-ups, each with a test that fails without it: a stated ladder is the whole offer (mapped aliases stay hidden); Ultra lowering keeps the stated ladder; listed Grok efforts replace the bundled profile; configured effort lists replace an inherited row profile.

Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi <hi@obviy.us>

commit.message:
fix: graceful restart exits within its deadline instead of waiting for systemd SIGKILL (#188188)

On Team (2026-10-30 05:05Z), the restart redesign resumed every running root correctly, but the process never exited on its own. systemd SIGKILLed it at 90 s:
- restart.close.session-admissions stayed pending for 85 s;
- a service-child relay (linux-subreaper) missed its cleanup deadline;
- the native hard-exit watchdog did not beat systemd.

Fixes:
- The session-admission join waited for full producer, operation, effect and terminal-persistence settlement. It now has a 5 s process-owned bound and keeps databases open for late cleanup.
- Service-child relay retirement: once descendant extinction is certified and channel closure is complete, it uses the existing direct-child retirement path.
- The hard-exit watchdog started its relative timer after worker bootstrap, which could exceed systemd's margin. It now consumes an absolute monotonic deadline and checks queued cancellation before killing.

Proof at exact head e0e9ee29edf3:
- Regressions for all three are red on base and green here. Close/resource suites (116), the service-child relay suite (36) and the hard-exit process test (incl. delayed cancellation and blocked-main SIGKILL) pass.
- The restart acceptance and handoff e2e pass: markers and abort in 24.6 ms, SIGTERM exit in 381 ms.
- Exact-head CI: 65 jobs succeeded, zero failed.

Gap: Linux handoff proof (Testbox queued). Uncertified owners still rely on the watchdog. Production +26 LOC.
